subject: ela
description: Students compare and contrast the experience of reading a story, drama, or poem with the experience of listening to or viewing an audio, video, or live version of that same text. They explain what each medium can show that the other cannot: print lets the reader picture characters, settings, and pace freely and gives direct access to a narrator's words and inner thoughts, while audio, film, or a live performance adds the sound of voices, music, tone, facial expressions, movement, lighting, and concrete images of people and places. Students identify which details a director, actor, narrator, or designer added, removed, or changed, and explain how those choices shape what an audience notices, feels, and understands. Because students cannot watch or listen during these items, every item embeds the written source it depends on and describes the audio, video, or live version in words within the item itself, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Distinguish the experience and tools of a written text (word choice, narration, reader's imagination, pace set by the reader) from those of an audio, video, or live version (voice, music, sound effects, visual images, acting, staging)
Identify what a specific medium can convey that another cannot (for example, a film shows a character's exact appearance; a book reveals a character's unspoken thoughts)
Determine how a director, actor, narrator, or designer interpreted the written text, including details they added, cut, emphasized, or altered
Explain how a media choice (a tone of voice, a piece of music, a camera angle, a costume, a stage set) changes what the audience notices, feels, or understands compared with reading the same moment
Compare and contrast the two experiences directly, naming a specific similarity and a specific difference grounded in the embedded text and the described version
Evaluate which medium is more effective for a particular purpose or moment and justify the judgment with reasons drawn from both the text and the description of the other version

problemArchetypes.name: Match a media tool to what only that medium can do
problemArchetypes.example: Read the line: 'Mara said she was fine, and she smiled as she said it.' In a film version, the actor playing Mara lets her voice shake and her eyes fill with tears on this line. What can the film show that the written line alone does not? Answer: The film reveals that Mara is not really fine; the shaking voice and tears let the audience see her hidden sadness, while the written line only reports her words and smile and leaves her true feeling for the reader to guess.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify a change the version made to the text
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'The old house stood silent at the end of the lane, its windows dark.' In an audio recording of this story, soft eerie music plays under the narrator's voice during this sentence. What has the audio version added that the written text does not include? Answer: It adds eerie background music, a sound the print cannot provide; the music makes the house feel frightening before anything scary has happened, while the written text describes only silence and dark windows.

problemArchetypes.name: Contrast a moment in print with the same moment performed
problemArchetypes.example: Read the stage direction and line from a drama: 'TOM (quietly): I never wanted any of this.' In a live performance, the actor playing Tom turns away from the other characters and lowers his head before he speaks. How does the live version's choice change this moment compared with reading it on the page? Answer: On the page the reader knows only that Tom speaks quietly, but in the live version his turning away and lowered head let the audience see his shame and his wish to hide, which the script's words alone do not show.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain a difference in what each medium leaves to the imagination
problemArchetypes.example: Read the description: 'The dragon was larger than any creature the villagers had ever seen.' In a movie version, the dragon is shown as a green, smoke-breathing beast the size of a barn. What is one difference between reading this and watching it? Answer: When reading, each person imagines the dragon's exact size and color, so it can look different to every reader; the movie fixes one image for everyone, which can feel more powerful but takes away the reader's freedom to picture the creature.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare how a poem reads silently versus heard aloud
problemArchetypes.example: Read the poem lines: 'Down, down, down the rain came, / drumming on the tin roof all night.' In an audio version, a reader speaks these lines slowly and a steady tapping sound plays behind the words. How does hearing this version compare with reading it on the page? Answer: Reading silently, the reader notices the repeated word 'down' and imagines the rain; the audio version adds the actual tapping sound and a slow pace, so the listener hears the rhythm of the rain instead of only picturing it, making the steady, sleepy feeling stronger.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge which medium better serves a purpose and justify
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt: 'In her mind, Lena replayed every word of the argument, sure she had ruined everything.' A film of this scene shows Lena sitting alone and staring at the floor. For showing what Lena is thinking, which version is more effective, and why? Answer: The written text is more effective here, because it states Lena's exact thoughts and her fear that she ruined everything; the film can show that she is upset but cannot directly reveal the words running through her mind, so the reader understands her inner experience more fully.

Easy.description: A short written stimulus of roughly 2 to 4 sentences (about 20 to 45 words) plus a one or two sentence description of a single, obvious media choice, both embedded in the item. The task is identify-level: name one clear thing the audio, video, or live version adds or shows that the text does not, or match a medium to the kind of detail it provides. The answer is supported by the surface contrast between the stated words and the described choice, with little inference required.
constraints: Stimulus is a 2 to 4 sentence excerpt or short poem lines included in the prompt, with simple vocabulary
The described media version contains one clear, obvious choice (a sound, an image, a tone of voice)
Identify-level task: name what one medium adds or shows that the other does not
Answer is supported by an explicit, surface contrast; minimal inference

Medium.description: A written passage of roughly 4 to 7 sentences (about 50 to 90 words) or a short poem stanza, plus a two or three sentence description of one or two media choices, all embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: explain how a specific media choice changes what the audience feels or understands compared with reading, or identify a detail the version added, cut, or altered and state its effect. The student must connect a particular choice in the described version to a particular effect, drawing on both the text and the description.
constraints: Stimulus is a 4 to 7 sentence passage or short poem stanza included in the prompt, grade-level vocabulary
The described version makes one or two choices whose effect is implied rather than stated
Analyze-level task: connect a specific media choice to how it changes the audience's understanding or feeling
Requires moderate inference; distractors are plausible partial or surface readings

Hard.description: A richer written passage of roughly 7 to 12 sentences (about 90 to 150 words) or a complete short poem, plus a fuller description of several interacting media choices (for example, acting, music, and staging together, or a version that changes the order or omits part of the text), all embedded in the item. The task is evaluate-level: compare and contrast the two experiences across the whole passage, judge which medium better serves a moment or purpose and justify it, or analyze how a version's interpretation shifts the meaning or feeling of the original. Requires sustained inference and synthesis of several details from both the text and the description.
constraints: Stimulus is a 7 to 12 sentence passage or a complete short poem included in the prompt, with some subtlety
The described version combines several choices, or reinterprets, reorders, or omits part of the text
Evaluate-level task: compare both experiences, judge effectiveness, or analyze a shift in meaning, citing multiple details
Requires sustained inference and synthesis across the whole passage and the full description

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes the audio, video, or live version is automatically better or more complete than the written text in every case
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the film or recording is superior because it 'shows everything,' ignoring what print does best, such as revealing a character's unspoken thoughts or letting the reader imagine freely

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the two versions as identical and lists only what they share, missing the contrast the standard requires
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States that the version is the same as the text because the plot or words match, without naming any difference in experience created by sound, image, or performance

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student credits a medium with a power it does not have, such as saying a written text lets you 'hear' a voice or that a silent image reveals exact thoughts
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Assigns to one medium a tool that belongs only to the other, for example claiming the book lets the reader hear the music or that the film directly shows the character's inner words

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student notices a media choice but cannot connect it to an effect, treating the difference as a fact with no consequence for meaning or feeling
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Correctly names a detail the version added or changed yet selects an explanation that does not link it to what the audience notices, feels, or understands

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a change the version made with something that was in the original text, blurring what was added, cut, or altered
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Attributes a music cue, camera choice, or actor's gesture to the written text itself, or claims the text included a detail that only the described version supplies

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student bases a judgment of which medium is better on personal preference alone, without reasons grounded in the text and the described version
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Justifies a choice with 'movies are more fun' or 'reading is boring' instead of reasons drawn from what each version actually conveys in the embedded example
